question: The Test Pyramid: What proportion of tests in a healthy codebase should be Unit Tests versus End-to-End (E2E) tests, and why?

options.text: Approximately 70% Unit Tests, 20% Integration Tests, and 10% E2E Tests. Unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint exact code failures, whereas E2E tests are slow, expensive to maintain, and brittle.
Approximately 70% E2E Tests, 20% Integration Tests, and 10% Unit Tests, because end-to-end coverage is what actually proves the product works for real users.
An even 33/33/33 split across Unit, Integration, and E2E tests is considered healthiest, since over-investing in any one layer creates blind spots in the others.
Unit tests should be avoided almost entirely (under 5%) in favor of Integration and E2E tests, because unit tests only verify implementation details that change too often to be worth maintaining.

explanation: Specification answer: Approximately 70% Unit Tests, 20% Integration Tests, and 10% E2E Tests. Unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint exact code failures, whereas E2E tests are slow, expensive to maintain, and brittle.

question: Assertion Rewriting: Why does pytest allow using plain Python assert a == b instead of requiring special assertion methods like self.assertEqual(a, b)?

options.text: pytest intercepts and rewrites Python's AST bytecode at test discovery time, extracting sub-expression values so that failing assert a == b statements print detailed visual diffs without verbose helper methods.
pytest requires every assert statement to be wrapped in a try/except block internally; the detailed diff output comes from parsing that exception's traceback, not from any AST rewriting.
Python's own assert statement natively prints variable values on failure in every context; pytest simply forwards this built-in behavior without doing any additional processing.
pytest replaces assert with a call to unittest.TestCase.assertEqual under the hood at import time, so the detailed diffs are actually produced by the unittest module, not by pytest itself.

explanation: Specification answer: pytest intercepts and rewrites Python's AST bytecode at test discovery time, extracting sub-expression values so that failing assert a == b statements print detailed visual diffs without verbose helper methods.

options.text: If an assertion fails inside a for loop, the test stops immediately and skips all remaining inputs. @pytest.mark.parametrize treats each parameter combination as an independent test case, reporting exact passes and failures for every single
@pytest.mark.parametrize runs faster because it executes all parameter combinations in a single test invocation using threads, while a for loop runs each iteration sequentially in the main thread.
The main advantage is that parametrize automatically generates the input values themselves (e.g. random integers), whereas a for loop requires the developer to hardcode every input by hand.

explanation: Specification answer: If an assertion fails inside a for loop, the test stops immediately and skips all remaining inputs. @pytest.mark.parametrize treats each parameter combination as an independent test case, reporting exact passes and failures for every single vector.

question: Fixture Scoping: What are the 4 fixture scopes supported by pytest, and what is the default scope?

options.text: 1. function (Default: runs fresh for every test function) 2. class (runs once per test class) 3. module (runs once per .py test file) 4. session (runs once per entire test suite execution)
1. session (Default: runs once for the whole suite) 2. module 3. class 4. function (runs once per test suite execution) -- broader scopes are preferred by default for speed.
1. function 2. module 3. package 4. global -- there is no class-scoped fixture; class-level setup must use unittest's setUp method instead.
pytest supports only two fixture scopes, function and session; class and module scoping were deprecated in pytest 7 in favor of explicit parametrize calls.

explanation: Specification answer: 1. function (Default: runs fresh for every test function) 2. class (runs once per test class) 3. module (runs once per .py test file) 4. session (runs once per entire test suite execution)
